# Claim, Tool, Vocabulary, Technique {#sec-four-columns}

Nine papers appear in this book, and the same pattern appears in all nine. **The specific claim is
weakened by later work, and something else in the paper survives and gets reused.**

Chapter 1's stable Paretian proposal was abandoned; the practice of looking at the tail survived.
Chapter 2's dimension values were shown to be method-dependent; the move from a quantity to its
scale behaviour survived. Chapter 20's optimal fraction is unusable without a discount; the interior
optimum survived.

A pattern that repeats nine times is worth a device. This chapter supplies one: a reading protocol
with four columns, and a rule about where to put your trust.

## The four columns

For any research result, fill four columns.

| Column | The question | How it ages |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Claim** | What does this assert about the world? | Decays as evidence accumulates |
| **Tool** | What does it make possible to ask or compute? | Usually outlives the claim |
| **Vocabulary** | What does it name that was unnamed? | Durable, but can be emptied by overuse |
| **Technique** | What procedure does it specify? | Durable until superseded |

The four behave differently. That is why four, not two.

**Claim and tool** are the pair that matters most. Two of four. A claim is a bet on how the world is arranged and
it can lose. A tool is equipment, and equipment gets reused by people who have no interest in the
original bet.

**Vocabulary is separate** for a reason. because naming does something that neither claims nor tools do: it
creates a category that others can use. "Fat tail", "black swan", "fourth quadrant" and "Kelly
fraction" are all instances. Their fate is different from a tool's, because a word can be used
correctly while the concept behind it is diluted. **A term that has been emptied of content still
appears in print**, which is why the vocabulary column needs its own line.

**Technique is separate** too. because it is the most concrete and the least durable in its details. A
specific estimation procedure is superseded by a better one, usually quietly.

## The test

The protocol is not a table to be admired. It has a test, and the test is what separates a real tool
column from a flattering one.

**Find a later paper that uses the tool while rejecting the claim.** If such a paper exists, the tool
column is real. If no such paper can be found, the tool column is probably imaginary — a
re-description of the claim in instrumental language.

Applying the test to the nine papers:

| Paper | Claim | Tool | A later user of the tool who rejected the claim |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Mandelbrot 1963 | Prices are stable Paretian | Look at the tail directly | The entire conditional-variance literature |
| Mandelbrot 1967 | Coastlines have dimension 1.25 | Measure a quantity's scale behaviour | Soil, image and network researchers |
| Mandelbrot and Van Ness 1968 | Series have long memory | Construct a process from desired properties | The rough-volatility literature, with the opposite sign |
| Taleb 2009 | Statistics fails in the fourth quadrant | Classify before choosing a method | Risk practitioners who ignore the quadrants |
| Taleb et al. 2014 | Precaution applies to GMOs and large nuclear | Screen on irreversibility | Vaccine and small-nuclear analysts who accept the screen |
| Cirillo and Taleb 2020 | The death-toll mean diverges | Ask about existence before precision | Any analyst reporting bounds |
| Thorp 1961 | Blackjack has favourable states | Look for state dependence | Option and market-microstructure work |
| Thorp 1969 | The optimal fraction is interior | Maximise growth rather than expected value | Institutional allocators who would reject the criterion |
| Thorp 1997 | Seven practical rules | Discount the theoretical fraction | Everyone who uses half-Kelly |

**The fourth column makes the protocol useful. Remember that.** A reader who fills only the first three
columns is doing literary analysis. A reader who has to name a later user of the tool while rejecting
the claim is checking whether the tool exists.

## The transfer rule

The protocol comes with a rule about trust.

**Trust transfers from the claim column to the tool column over time, and the transfer should be
deliberate rather than automatic.** Specifically:

**Immediately after publication**, the claim is the most informative part, because it is the author's
assertion about the world and the author knows more about it than the reader does.

**After a decade**, the tool is usually the more informative part, because the claim has been tested
and the tests are public, while the tool has been used and its uses are visible.

**The transfer should be gradual, and it should be slowed by evidence about the claim.** A claim that
has survived replication keeps its claim-column value longer. **The failure mode is transferring
early — abandoning a claim because it is unfashionable, or keeping it because the tool is useful.**

## Failure modes

Three, and the third is the one I have committed.

**Imaginary tool columns.** Catch them. Describing a claim in instrumental language and calling it a tool. The
test above catches this if it is applied honestly, which is why the test requires a named later
paper rather than a plausible category of user.

**Retrospective tool attribution.** Common in books like this one. Reading a tool into a paper that did not actually contain it,
because the tool seems to follow from the paper's conclusions. This is a specific hazard for books
about ideas rather than about methods, and it is why the tool columns above name techniques that
appear in the papers rather than implications a reader might draw.

**Using the protocol to excuse failed claims.** The trap. A reader who has learned the protocol can say "the
claim failed but the tool survived" about almost anything, and the sentence has the form of an
insight while being a refusal to update. **The discipline that prevents this is writing down what the
tool could not do** — a column I have not included, and on reflection should have.

## The protocol applied to itself

**What transformation should it survive?** Changes of domain: it should apply to papers in medicine,
engineering, and the social sciences.

**Does it?** The four columns are general. The trust-transfer rule is general. What does not travel
is the ease of the test: in fields where subsequent work is not indexed, or where methods are not
cited explicitly, naming a later user of the tool while rejecting the claim may be impossible.

**Verdict.** A grade II construction.

## Claim and tool

The claim: research results decompose into four components with different lifespans, and confusion
between them explains both the persistence of failed claims and the discarding of useful tools.

The tool: the four columns, the naming test, and the gradual transfer rule.

Registered as B-006, with the failure modes above attached.

## Boundary conditions

The protocol applies to research results that make claims about the world. Purely methodological
papers — a new estimator, a new algorithm — have an empty claim column, and forcing them into the
protocol produces an artificial entry.

It presumes that subsequent literature can be searched, which excludes very recent work and work in
fields with thin citation records.

And it does not evaluate. The protocol tells you what is likely to survive, not what is true.

## Filling the columns on a paper from this book

The protocol is best learned by applying it to something whose status is already documented, and the
book supplies nine candidates. Take the fourth-quadrant paper.

**The claim. Contested at its boundary.** That standard statistical methods fail in the fourth
quadrant. The book's own reading is that the paper's two-axis structure is precise and its most-quoted
formulation is not verifiable, which is why the grade is II with a contested boundary rather than I.

**The tool. Widely used.** The two-by-two classification, applied before a method is chosen. Its users
include practitioners who have never read the paper and who would reject parts of its argument.

**The vocabulary. Diluted.** "Fourth quadrant" and "black swan" name something that was previously
unnamed, and both are now used in ways the paper does not license. **The words survived while the
constraints on their use did not.**

**The technique. Thin.** The paper does not specify an estimation procedure, which is why the tool
column is a classification rather than a method. This is worth noticing: **not every paper has all four
columns populated, and an empty technique column is a finding about the paper rather than a gap in the
analysis.**

**What the exercise shows.** The four columns separate cleanly on a paper the book has already
analysed, which is the weakest possible test. **The test that matters is applying it to a paper whose
status is unknown, and the protocol's value there is that it forces the fourth column — the naming of a
later user — to be attempted rather than assumed.**

## Where the protocol fails as a research tool

The protocol is a reading device. Used as a research instrument it has three failure modes, and the
book has committed the first two.

**It rewards the searchable.** The fourth column requires naming a later user of the tool while
rejecting the claim. Where the literature is well indexed, this is easy; where it is not, the column
stays empty and the tool appears imaginary. **The protocol therefore systematically underrates results
in fields with poor citation records.**

**It confuses absence with failure.** A tool that has not yet been reused may be new rather than
imaginary. The protocol cannot distinguish the two without waiting, and waiting is not available when
the reading is being done now.

**It invites retrospective attribution.** This is the failure named in the chapter and it is the easiest
to commit: reading a tool into a paper because the tool seems to follow from the paper's conclusions.
The defence is to require a technique that appears in the paper's own text, which is a much stricter
test than a plausible implication.

**What the protocol is good for.** Deciding how much weight to give a result in a literature review,
and noticing when a claim is doing work that its evidence cannot support. **It is a reading discipline,
not a discovery method, and the distinction should be stated by anyone who adopts it.**

**One gap, restated.** The chapter noted the absence of a column for what a tool cannot do, and the
case above shows why it matters. A tool's limits are what determine whether it can be carried into a
new domain, and the four columns as drawn provide no place to record them.

## The columns for a paper you are about to use

The protocol is presented as a reading device for finished literature. Its most practical application is
to a paper whose result you intend to rely on.

**Four questions, in order.**

**One. What exactly would I be relying on?** Not what the paper claims, but which sentence or result your
decision would use. **Most of the time it is narrower than the paper's title suggests.**

**Two. Which column does my reliance sit in?** If you are relying on the claim, you are betting on the
boundary holding. If on the tool, the claim's fate is less important. **Naming the column tells you what
to monitor.**

**Three. Who else has used this, and for what?** A tool with many users has been stress-tested by use. A
claim with many citers may have been quoted without being tested, and the distinction is invisible in a
citation count.

**Four. What would have to happen for my reliance to be misplaced?** A test of the boundary, a mechanism
change, a better estimator. **This is the monitoring specification, and writing it takes a paragraph.**

**What the four questions prevent.** The most common error in applied work, which is relying on a result
without knowing which part of it is doing the work. **A practitioner who has answered question two knows
whether they need the boundary to hold or only the technique to exist, and those require different
responses to the same new evidence.**

**Where the protocol is least useful.** On papers whose result you will not rely on. **The columns are
for the small number of results that enter a decision, and applying them to everything read is the
failure mode the chapter's second section describes.**

## The four columns for a method rather than a result

The protocol is presented for results. Methodological work has a different profile, and the difference is worth
one section because methods are what most practitioners actually adopt.

**The columns for a method.**

**Claim. Often absent.** A new estimator may carry no claim about the world. **An empty claim column is normal
here, unlike in substantive work.**

**Tool. Central.** The estimator or procedure itself. **A method's tool column is its content.**

**Vocabulary. Rare.** Methods rarely name anything.

**Technique. Detailed.** The implementation, the parameters, the failure modes.

**What the asymmetry implies for reading.**

**A method is judged on its technique column.** Whether it works under this data, at this sample size, with
these assumptions. **The question is not whether it is elegant but whether the practitioner's data resemble
the conditions under which it was validated.**

**A method's claim column, where present, deserves scrutiny.** A method paper that claims domain-general
validity has made an empirical claim alongside a procedure, and the claim is usually weaker than the
procedure.

**A method that survives its claim is the normal case.** Methods outlive the problems they were designed for,
which is the same pattern as tools outliving claims in the substantive literature.

**One practical test. Two datasets.** Apply the method to the researcher's data and to a synthetic dataset with
known properties. **Where it fails on the synthetic one, the failure mode is visible; where it succeeds on
both, the confidence is warranted. The exercise takes an afternoon and is the equivalent of the fourth column
for a method.**

## Two rows filled for the book itself

The protocol applies to other people's work. Applying it to this book is the shortest demonstration that it is
a discipline rather than a rhetorical device.

**The book's claim column. Contested.** That nine results were weakened in their claims while their tools
survived. **The register is the evidence and the reading is the author's; a reader who checks the entries and
finds the claims standing is entitled to dismiss the framing.**

**The book's tool column. Four constructions and one protocol.** The Constant's grades, the grid, the discount,
the ledger, the ordering, and the four-column protocol itself. **All are untested, and the constructed register
says so on every row.**

**The book's vocabulary column. Borrowed and redefined.** Several terms are used in narrower senses than
ordinary usage, and the glossary fixes them. **A reader who substitutes the ordinary sense will misread several
chapters, which is the cost of the book's terminology and is disclosed rather than avoided.**

**The book's technique column. Scripts and registers.** Figure generation, the prose gate, the register
validator, the build-input check. **These are the parts of the book that a reader can execute, and they are
the only parts whose claims are mechanically verifiable.**

**What the four rows show. One asymmetry.** The book's verified material is in its claims column, and its
novelty is in its tools and vocabulary. **A reader who wants to accept the reading and reject the
constructions can do so cleanly, because the two are kept apart in the files.**

**Why the exercise is worth running on one's own work.** Because the pattern is easier to see from outside.
**An author who has filled the four columns for nine other people's results and then for the book itself will
notice which column carries the weight, and it is usually not the one they were most proud of.**

## The protocol and the three layers

The protocol has been applied to nine papers and to this book. Its relation to the book's three-layer structure
is worth one section, because the two devices describe the same material from different directions.

**The layers. Worldview, knowledge, action.** The constraint runs downward: the world constrains models,
models constrain stakes, stakes constrain opportunities.

**The columns. Claim, tool, vocabulary, technique.** The ageing runs sideways: claims decay, tools are reused,
vocabulary dilutes, technique is superseded.

**What each device is for. Different questions.**

The layers answer "may I use this method for this decision". **They are a filter on application.**

The columns answer "what part of this result should I keep". **They are a filter on reading.**

**Where they meet. One place.** A tool that survives a claim is a tool that has been carried across a layer
boundary. **The tail argument from the worldview layer survives into the action layer as the screening rule,
and the columns register that survival as the tool column being populated while the claim column empties.**

**What the meeting implies for a reader. One practice.** After applying the columns, ask which layer the
surviving tool belongs to. **A tool that survives at the worldview layer licenses a model; one that survives at
the action layer licenses a decision; the difference determines what the reader may do with it.**

**Why both devices are needed.** The layers have no temporal dimension and the columns have no application
dimension. **A reader with only the layers cannot tell which parts of an abandoned paper to keep; a reader with
only the columns cannot tell which surviving tool applies to the decision in front of them.**

**What neither device supplies.** The mechanism. **Both are filters, and a filter tells you what passes rather
than why it does, which is why the chapters that use them are organised around mechanisms rather than around
the two tables.**

## The protocol as a defence against the confident summary

The four columns have a use that is not about research at all: they are a defence against the confident summary
in a meeting.

**The situation. Common.** A colleague states a result with assurance, and it is the assurance rather than the
result that carries the room.

**What the protocol supplies. Three questions.**

**Which column is that from?** If the claim is the source of the confidence, the boundary matters. If it is a
technique, the boundary may be irrelevant. **The question separates two things that sound identical.**

**Who else has used it?** A tool with many users has been tested by use. **A claim with many citers may merely
have been quoted, and the distinction is invisible in the assurance.**

**What would make it wrong?** The fourth column's question. **A speaker who can answer it has understood the
result; one who cannot has memorised it.**

**Why the questions work in a meeting. Two reasons.**

**They are procedural rather than adversarial.** Asking which column is like asking which section of a document,
and the answer is informative rather than a challenge.

**They take ten seconds each.** Which matters more than depth, because the moment for the question is the moment
of the claim.

**What they do not do.** Resolve the dispute. **A confident speaker with a well-understood grade II claim is
usually right, and the questions establish that rather than undermining it.**

**Where the protocol fails in this role.** When the room has no patience for procedure. **In that setting the
questions read as obstruction, and there is no version of this material that works without a listener willing to
ask one of them.**

**Why the framing is worth stating.** Because the book's apparatus is usually described as an analytical method,
and its most frequent use in practice is social: it changes what can be said with assurance in a room where
decisions are made.

## The columns for a claim you intend to repeat

The protocol is described for reading. Its most consequential use is before repeating a claim, which is what
most writing and speaking consists of.

**The situation. Common.** A claim is about to be repeated in a document, a talk or a decision memo. **The
repetition is where most claims travel, and it is where their conditions are dropped.**

**Three checks before repeating.**

**Which column is being repeated?** A claim or a tool. **A tool can be repeated without its originating claim;
a claim cannot be repeated without its boundary, because the boundary is part of the claim.**

**What is the boundary, in one clause?** The range, the population, the method. **If no clause comes to mind,
the claim has been memorised rather than understood.**

**Who else repeats it, and how?** Which tells you whether the repetition is customary in the field or an
innovation of yours. **Customary repetitions have usually shed their conditions already, which is why the
literature's most quoted sentences are its least qualified.**

**What the checks change about the output. One thing.** The repeated sentence gets a clause. **"Tail risk
matters" becomes "over the ranges measured, extremes are more frequent than a normal implies". The second
sentence is longer and it can be checked.**

**What repetition does to a claim over time. Two effects.**

**Conditions erode.** Each repetition is shorter than the last, and the boundary is the first thing to go.

**Authority accumulates.** A claim repeated by many acquires weight without acquiring evidence. **The process is
the mechanism behind grade inflation, and it operates on writers who mean to be careful.**

**What a writer can do about it. One habit.** Attach the boundary to the claim at the moment of first use in a
document, and then use the short form. **The reader who has seen the boundary once can carry it; the reader who
has never seen it will supply their own, usually a stronger one.**

**Why the protocol belongs at the point of writing rather than at the point of reading.** Because the erosion
happens on the way out. **A reader's discipline can recover a boundary from a source; a writer's omission
cannot be recovered by anyone downstream.**

## The four columns and three kinds of doubt

A reader who doubts a result can doubt the claim, the tool, or the reading. The columns localise the doubt, and
the localisation determines what would resolve it.

**Doubt about the claim. The common case.** The result is contested or its boundary is narrow. **Which the columns
handle by placing the doubt in a column and asking what else in the row depends on it: a tool with many users can
survive a claim's failure, and the reader's reliance may be on the tool.**

**Doubt about the tool. Rarer and more serious.** The method does not do what it claims. **Which is a question
about the method's validation and is answered by the technique column, not by the claim's record.**

**Doubt about the reading. The reader's own.** The paper may not say what the reader took it to say. **Which the
columns handle by requiring the claim to be stated in the reader's words before the other three columns are
filled.**

**What the three have in common. One property.** Each is resolved by a different body of evidence: the literature
for the claim, the method's validation for the tool, and the paper's text for the reading. **Which is why
localising the doubt is the first step rather than a formality.**

**Which doubt is most often misattributed. The third.** Because a reader's misreading presents as a doubt about
the claim, and the correction is a re-reading rather than more evidence. **Which is the cheapest resolution
available and the one least often attempted.**

**How to use the columns against doubt. One order.** State the reliance, then the column, then the evidence that
would resolve it. **Three sentences, and the doubt becomes a question with an answer rather than a
disposition.**

**Why the columns are worth this treatment.** Because their value is not classification but the localisation of
disagreement. **Three kinds of doubt, three bodies of evidence, and the columns are what assign them.**

## A note on what this chapter could not check

The protocol is proposed by this book. The nine worked rows use material documented in Parts I to
III, and the fourth column in each row is my judgement about which later literature used the tool. I
have not verified that any specific paper in that column uses the earlier tool while rejecting the
earlier claim; the column is a research instruction rather than a citation.

The observation that I should have added a column for what the tool cannot do is left in the text
rather than corrected, because the omission and its recognition are both part of the argument.
